questions.intro: Privacy rules can apply to data used with AI. Two dated examples. In the United States, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule (COPPA) covers personal information collected online from children under 13; the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) amended it in 2025, with most compliance required by April 22, 2026. In the European Union, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, since 2018), in Article 22, gives people a right not to be subject to decisions based SOLELY on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects, with stated exceptions and safeguards. Rules differ by place.

questions.prompt: "Records children's voices" answers which question?
questions.intro: Most privacy rules ask five questions about personal data. (1) WHAT is collected? (2) WHY, for what purpose? (3) CONSENT or NOTICE: were people told or asked? (4) WHO receives it? (5) HOW LONG is it kept? Example: a reading app records children's voices (what) to measure fluency (why), tells parents and asks permission (consent), shares recordings only with the teacher (who), and deletes them after the school year (how long).

questions.prompt: "To measure fluency" answers which question?

choices.text: Who receives the data, because teachers are the ones who measure the fluency

choices.text: None, because COPPA is the only privacy rule that exists anywhere in the United States
State privacy laws and sector laws

questions.intro: Privacy rules usually ask similar questions: What personal data is collected? For what purpose? Did people consent or get notice? Who receives it? How long is it kept? Many US states have their own privacy laws, and sector laws cover areas such as health and education records. When an AI project uses personal data, collect only what is needed, tell people, protect it, and check which rules apply where you are. This is general information, not legal advice.
